title: What special education and dose limits apply to radiation workers in Japan?
description: Japan's Ionizing Radiation Hazards Ordinance: special education for X-ray and gamma work (widened April 2026), 4.5 hours, and the 2021 eye lens dose limit.
shortAnswer: Japan's Ordinance on Prevention of Ionizing Radiation Hazards requires employers to give special education before workers handle X-ray or gamma ray equipment, nuclear fuel or accident waste. From April 1, 2026, the X-ray and gamma course covers all handling work except fully shielded box units, with at least 4.5 hours of classroom teaching. Since April 1, 2021, the eye lens dose limit has been 100 mSv over five years and 50 mSv in any year.
keyTakeaways: Article 59(3) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act requires special education before hazardous work, and Articles 52-5 to 52-9 of the Ordinance on Prevention of Ionizing Radiation Hazards set the subjects for five radiation work categories.
MHLW Ordinance No. 108 of 2025 widened the X-ray and gamma course from radiography only to all work handling X-ray or gamma irradiation equipment, except box-type units, from April 1, 2026.
MHLW Notice No. 287 of 2025 sets the minimum classroom hours: 1.5 for work methods, 1.5 for equipment structure and handling, 0.5 for biological effects and 1.0 for laws, a total of 4.5 hours.
The eye lens equivalent dose limit fell from 150 mSv a year to 100 mSv over five years and 50 mSv in any year on April 1, 2021; the transitional relief for certain physicians ended on March 31, 2026.
Special education records must be kept for three years; individual dose records must be kept for 30 years, or five years before transfer to a designated body.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) Industrial Safety and Health Department, enforced by Prefectural Labor Bureaus and Labor Standards Inspection Offices
appliesTo: Employers whose workers handle X-ray equipment or gamma irradiation equipment, in industry, research and, on the text of the ordinance, health care
Employers at nuclear fuel processing, reprocessing, use and reactor facilities
Employers handling accident-derived waste and those assigning staff to specified emergency work
Radiation workers (hōshasen gyōmu jūjisha), their supervisors and X-ray work chiefs

sections.heading: Where does the radiation special education duty come from?

blocks.text: The duty starts in Article 59(3) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法, Act No. 57 of 1972), which requires employers to give special education before assigning workers to dangerous or harmful work specified by ministerial ordinance. Article 36 of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health (労働安全衛生規則) lists that work, including item 28 (X-ray and gamma irradiation equipment) and items 28-2 onward (nuclear facilities and related work) ([Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347M50002000032)). The general system is covered in [Japan's special education for hazardous work](/regulations/japan-special-education-for-hazardous-work).

The radiation-specific content is in the **Ordinance on Prevention of Ionizing Radiation Hazards** (電離放射線障害防止規則, Ministry of Labour Ordinance No. 41 of 1972), Chapter 6-2. It also sets dose limits, dose measurement and record duties for radiation workers, meaning workers engaged in radiation work in a controlled area ([Ionizing Radiation Ordinance, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347M50002000041)).

sections.heading: Which radiation work requires special education?

blocks.text: Five categories, each with its own syllabus under the Ionizing Radiation Ordinance:

blocks.caption: Special education categories in Chapter 6-2 of the Ordinance on Prevention of Ionizing Radiation Hazards
head: Article
Work
Subjects
rows: Handling X-ray equipment or gamma irradiation equipment, except equipment whose controlled area is only inside a shielded enclosure that no part of a worker's body enters during irradiation
Work methods; equipment structure and handling; biological effects of ionizing radiation; relevant laws
Handling nuclear fuel material, spent fuel or contaminated items in controlled areas of processing, reprocessing or use facilities
Materials; work methods; facility equipment; biological effects; laws; practical training in work methods and equipment handling
Handling nuclear fuel material, spent fuel or contaminated items in controlled areas of reactor facilities
Specified emergency work assigned to nuclear emergency personnel

blocks.text: For each category, detailed hours are set by MHLW notice under the article's second paragraph. Article 37 of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health lets employers omit subjects for workers recognized as having sufficient knowledge and skills, and Article 38 requires a record of attendees and subjects to be kept for three years.

sections.heading: What changed for X-ray and gamma equipment on April 1, 2026?

blocks.text: The scope widened from radiography to all handling work. MHLW Ordinance No. 108 of 2025, promulgated October 29, 2025, amended Article 36(28) of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health and Article 52-5 of the Ionizing Radiation Ordinance with effect from April 1, 2026. Before that date, special education applied only to "radiography using X-ray equipment or gamma irradiation equipment" (tōka shashin satsuei, mainly non-destructive testing). From that date it applies to work handling X-ray or gamma irradiation equipment generally, excluding box-type equipment whose controlled area exists only inside a shielded enclosure ([MHLW Ordinance No. 108 of 2025](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001587771.pdf)).

MHLW Notice No. 287 of 2025 renamed the training rules as the Special Education Rules for Work Handling X-ray Equipment and Gamma Irradiation Equipment (エックス線装置及びガンマ線照射装置取扱業務特別教育規程), applied from April 1, 2026. Workers who completed the old radiography course need not be retrained for radiography work ([MHLW Notice No. 287 of 2025](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001587781.pdf)). MHLW's leaflet adds that workers newly brought into scope may have overlapping subjects omitted under Article 37 if they already took the radiography course or education under other laws, and sets out the minimum hours ([MHLW leaflet on the expanded scope](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001587812.pdf)):

items: knowledge of work methods for X-ray or gamma equipment (work procedures, radiation measurement, exposure prevention, accident response): 1.5 hours;

knowledge of equipment structure and handling (X-ray tube, high-voltage generator and controller, operation and inspection; or gamma source container, remote handling and source properties): 1.5 hours;
biological effects of ionizing radiation on cells, tissues, organs and the whole body: 0.5 hours; and
relevant provisions of the Industrial Safety and Health Act, its Cabinet Order and ordinances: 1.0 hour.

blocks.text: The same ordinance added duties for X-ray and gamma radiography work chiefs from April 1, 2026, including deciding work methods to minimize exposure and directing radiation workers, and requires automatic alarms and fail-safe safety devices on industrial X-ray equipment in radiation rooms from October 1, 2027, with transitional measures for equipment that cannot be modified ([MHLW summary leaflet](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001713846.pdf)). As at November 2026 the safety device duties have not commenced.

blocks.title: Health care employers
blocks.text: The amended text of Article 52-5 excludes only box-type equipment and contains no exclusion for medical X-ray equipment, while the ordinance separately recognizes medical equipment managed under the Medical Care Act. Hospitals and clinics should confirm with their Labor Standards Inspection Office how the expanded scope applies to radiological technologists and other staff, and which subjects can be omitted under Article 37 for licensed professionals.

sections.heading: What did the 2021 eye lens dose limit change?

blocks.text: MHLW Ordinance No. 82 of 2020 lowered the occupational limit for equivalent dose to the lens of the eye from April 1, 2021. Article 5 previously set 150 mSv a year. It now requires employers to keep radiation workers' lens dose within 100 mSv over five years and 50 mSv in any one year, alongside 500 mSv a year for skin. The effective dose limits in Article 4 are unchanged: 100 mSv over five years and 50 mSv in any year, and 5 mSv per three months for women who may become pregnant.

The amending ordinance gave relief to certain physicians whose lens dose could exceed 100 mSv over five years despite shielding, whose work needs advanced expertise and who cannot easily be replaced: 50 mSv a year only until March 31, 2023, then 60 mSv over three years until March 31, 2026. MHLW's leaflet said employers had to designate these physicians by March 31, 2023, after review by the health committee, and keep the designation records until March 31, 2026 ([MHLW 2021 leaflet](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/000753878.pdf)). That relief has now ended, so as at November 2026 the full limit applies to every radiation worker.

Measurement and records changed too. Lens dose is in principle calculated from the 3 mm dose equivalent, and Article 9(2)(v) requires lens dose totals for every three months, every year and every five years to be recorded. MHLW's leaflet notes that readings taken inside protective eyewear may be used, and that the cataract eye examination in radiation health checks should not be omitted for workers whose lens dose exceeded 20 mSv in the previous year and may exceed 20 mSv in the current year.

sections.heading: Which training and dose records must be kept, and for how long?

blocks.text: Training records and dose records have different clocks. Special education records (attendees and subjects) must be kept for three years under Article 38 of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health. Dose records under Article 9(2) of the Ionizing Radiation Ordinance must be calculated, recorded and kept for 30 years, unless after five years they are handed to an institution designated by the Minister, and the results must be given to each worker without delay under Article 9(3). The difference matters when designing records: see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

blocks.text: Training content on biological effects is the natural place to explain the lens limit, dosimeter placement and protective eyewear, since those behaviors drive compliance with Articles 5 and 8.

Labor Standards Inspection Offices enforce both the special education duty and the dose limits during workplace inspections. Failure to give special education is a breach of Article 59(3) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act, punishable under Article 119 of the Act by imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 500,000 yen, and inspectors issue correction notices for missing training or dose records. Separate patient-side radiation safety duties for hospitals sit under the Medical Care Act; see [Japan's hospital medical safety training](/regulations/japan-hospital-medical-safety-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each special education article, the notice hours and the dose provisions as obligations tied to roles and equipment types, so a change such as the April 2026 scope expansion shows exactly which roles need bridging. Learning outcomes and assessments are defined per subject before content is written.

faqs.q: How long is the X-ray and gamma special education course in Japan?
faqs.a: At least 4.5 hours of classroom teaching under the special education rules applied from April 1, 2026: 1.5 hours on work methods, 1.5 hours on equipment structure and handling, 0.5 hours on biological effects and 1.0 hour on laws. Subjects can be omitted for workers with sufficient knowledge under Article 37 of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health.

faqs.q: Do workers trained under the old radiography course need retraining?
faqs.a: Not for radiography work. MHLW Notice No. 287 of 2025 states that workers trained under the pre-amendment radiography rules need no further special education to continue radiography. Workers moving into other X-ray or gamma handling work may have overlapping subjects omitted.

faqs.q: Is the eye lens dose limit 20 mSv a year in Japan?
faqs.a: The limit is 100 mSv over five years and 50 mSv in any single year, which averages 20 mSv a year. It has applied since April 1, 2021, and the transitional relief for certain physicians ended on March 31, 2026.

faqs.q: Does fully enclosed X-ray inspection equipment need special education?
faqs.a: No. Article 52-5 excludes work using equipment whose controlled area exists only inside the unit and which is shielded so that no part of a worker's body enters it during irradiation, typically box-type inspection units.
